News Report One.

The hottest day of September on record pushed the city of Tucson to activate its emergency heat plan for the first time this year, opening nine cooling centers in libraries, community colleges and fire stations.
The National Weather Service logged 41 degrees Celsius downtown shortly before three in the afternoon, one degree above the previous mark from 2006.
Officials urged residents to ride free municipal buses between errands rather than walk, and public pools stayed open two hours longer than usual.
Utilities warned that pressure on the electrical grid would remain tight until evening, when air-conditioner use peaks.
City hospitals reported twenty-two heat-related admissions, most of them over the age of seventy.
The mayor said shaded bus stops and four thousand additional street trees would go before the council in November, together with money to insulate the homes of low-income families.
News Report Two.
A regional museum that had kept almost all of its collection in boxes has reopened with a complete online catalogue and free handheld guides.

The Riverside Institute spent four point two million dollars over four years photographing each of its thirty-eight thousand objects; the images are now downloadable, and teachers have been using them to build classroom lessons.
Only about nine hundred pieces hang in the galleries, though curators promise to rotate the displays twice a year.
Visitors may bring their own telephones or take a device from the front desk to summon pictures, recordings and descriptions in six languages.

The director said the goal was to reach people who rarely walk through museum doors: downloads from other countries now make up about a third of the traffic, and school groups arrived twenty percent more often during the first term.
Admission stays free on Sundays.
News Report Three.
Owners of small shops and workshops say they cannot absorb another rise in electricity costs, according to a survey published on Monday by a regional business federation.

Nearly seven in ten of the thirteen hundred firms questioned reported bills more than double what they paid two years earlier, and a quarter said they had already reduced staff hours or shut one site.
The federation is asking the national regulator to postpone a scheduled change in wholesale pricing until spring and to extend short-term credit.
Large manufacturers, by contrast, have protected themselves with longer contracts and expect smaller increases.
Owners of bakeries and laundries told reporters they were weighing higher prices, which they fear could push shoppers toward supermarket chains.
The regulator answered that it reviews tariffs twice a year and that support schemes for vulnerable customers are already open.
Conversation One.

Medical school, ideally, though I hate the thought of writing all year.

The sections run Tuesday evenings and Friday afternoons; the Tuesday one collides with your lab, so you'd want Friday.

Conversation Two.

Passage One.
For thirty years the distance an average American drives each day has barely changed, while the share of trips taken on foot has fallen to about one in fifty.
Researchers in Melbourne decided to test whether the built environment could push that number the other way, and their findings are now changing how several cities approve new housing.
The study followed more than two thousand adults for three years, mapping every street within a kilometer of their homes and asking them to record where they actually went on foot.
The strongest predictor turned out not to be parks or scenery but something drier: how many crossings a person needed to reach the next block.
Districts built on long superblocks, where a shop sits two kilometers away behind a wall of garages, produced almost no walking at all, whatever residents said about their intentions.
Small blocks with frequent intersections kept people on their feet, and the effect held after the researchers allowed for income, age and whether a household owned a car.
A second result was less obvious: steps gathered in a few repeatable spots, so benches, shade and safe crossings brought outsize benefits where they were placed.
Planners now argue that laying pavement beside existing wide roads achieves far less than cutting those roads into shorter pieces.
Passage Two.
Ask a student how to prepare for an examination and most will answer with late nights and strong coffee.
Ask a neuroscientist and you are likely to hear the opposite.

During deep sleep the brain runs through the day's events at high speed, a process researchers call consolidation, and in doing so it carries fragile new information out of a temporary holding area and into permanent storage.
In one well-known experiment, volunteers learned a sequence of finger taps and were tested twelve hours later.
Half of them slept during that interval and half stayed awake.
The rested group improved by roughly ten percent on average, and the gains were still there a week later, while repetition with no sleep in between produced almost nothing.
A second finding is stranger, because rest appears to choose.

Not everything learned between breakfast and bedtime survives; cues presented around a study session, such as a particular smell or a brief tone, can tip which traces are kept, and anything tagged as emotionally important is pushed to the front of the queue.
That helps explain why a student who works four hours and then sleeps often does better than one who works eight and does not.
It also explains a cruelty in the same mechanism: an all-nighter damages recall of precisely the material the extra hours were meant to protect.
Passage Three.
How does a monarch butterfly, which has never made the journey, find a mountain valley it visited only in its ancestry?
The answer, increasingly, is that the route arrives preloaded.

Monarchs crossing North America live in a chain of generations: the individuals that travel thousands of kilometers are great-great-grandchildren of those that left the same valleys the previous autumn.

Field experiments with raised nets and displaced adults show that the insects combine a sun compass, which needs clear light, with an internal clock, so that they can correct for the sun's travel across the sky.
Cloudy days do not stop them, because they also read polarization, a pattern in the light that survives cloud and that human eyes cannot detect.
Pigeons turn out to be even less single-minded.
They use the Earth's magnetic field, odors carried along familiar routes and possibly low-frequency sound, and when researchers blocked one channel the birds simply relied on the rest.
The most surprising navigation belongs to the desert ant, which keeps a tally of its own strides.
Scientists glued hair-thin extensions to some animals' legs and shortened others by amputation; the foragers then overshot or fell short of their nests by exactly the amount the alteration predicted.
No one has found an insect that uses only one sense to get home.
